newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour sets course for landslide victory.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour sets course for landslide victory.

text.p: Tony Blair was poised on Friday to become Britain's youngest prime minister this century on the back of a landslide victory for his new-look Labour Party on a scale unseen for 165 years.
The BBC predicted Labour would end 18 years of Conservative rule that have transformed Britain by grabbing a majority of 203 in the 659-seat parliament, a margin unseen since 1832.
Recriminations began to fly in John Major's Conservative Party as it headed for opposition after the longest period of single party government in Britain this century.
"There has been nothing like it this century. It is a like an asteroid destroying practically all life on earth," politics professor Anthony King said.
On initial results, shortly before midnight GMT, Labour had won 32 constituencies on an average swing of 9.6 percent, and the Conservatives had yet to win one.
"I am sure these exit polls are exaggerated, but it does look like a good win and obviously I am very pleased," Peter Mandelson, who organised Labour's campaign, told ITN.
Seconds after voting ended at 2100 GMT on Thursday, ITN commercial television said Labour could have a majority of 159 seats on a swing to Labour from the Conservatives of 12.2 percent.
The BBC's exit polls gave Labour 47 percent support, 29 percent for the Conservatives and 18 percent for the centre-left Liberal Democrats.
"I think the mood of the country was for a change after 18 years in power," Sir David Steel, former leader of the Liberal Democrats, said.
Evidence that the exit polls were close to the mark came when the seat of Crosby in northwest England -- 120th on Labour's target list -- fell to Blair's party with a swing of 10 percent.
The seat of Edgbaston in Birmingham, central England, also fell to Labour for the first time, with its German-born candidate Gisela Stewart recording a 10 percent swing.
There were early signs that defeat would lead to a bloodbath in the Conservative Party, which prides itself in being one of the most effective political machines in the world.

Over 18 years, first under "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher and then under Major, the Conservatives transformed Britain, halting decades of relative economic decline by privatising vast swathes of industry and taming powerful trade unions.

Major's appeal to voters was "better the devil you know than the devil you don't", but deep divisions over Europe, broken promises over tax and allegations of sleaze in the ruling party meant he had a Herculean task.
"If the polls are right and we have actually lost, then there will have to be a lot of questions asked and answers to give," Deputy Prime Minister Michael Heseltine said.
Heseltine is one of several Conservatives who are likely to throw their hat in the ring if a big defeat is confirmed and Major steps down after 6-1/2 years as head of the party.
Another likely challenger, outgoing Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, admitted that the past five years of bitter infighting over Europe had cost the party dear.
"I think what the party needs to reflect upon is that it has done itself no good by showing its divisions," he said.
"It is clear that going Eurosceptic did not help the Conservatives one jot," Edwina Currie, a pro-European, said.

Nicholas Winterton, a Euro-sceptic Conservative fiercely opposed to closer ties with Brussels, put the blame firmly at the door of Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance minister) Kenneth Clarke for refusing to rule out the possibility that Britain might sign up one day for the European Union's planned single currency.
"He will be remembered, even reviled in history for his actions," Winterton said.
Victory would be a ringing endorsement for Blair's crusade, since he became Labour leader in 1993, to dump the left-wing policies that led it to four successive election defeats.
Blair, 43, would be the youngest prime minister this century. He was a student at Oxford University when Labour last won a British election in 1974.
Blair has promised change -- but not too much change -- with a programme some commentators have dubbed Conservatism with a human face.
